content:
JavaScript: 5. The V8 Engine

V8 is Google's open-source high-performance JS engine written in C++. It parses JavaScript, translates it to an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), and uses Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation to convert it directly to fast machine code.

topic: 6. let vs const: When to use which
content:
JavaScript: 6. let vs const

Default to const for variables to prevent reassignment and signal immutability of the reference. Use let strictly when you anticipate the variable's value changing, like loop counters.

Example:

topic: 7. var and the dangers of Hoisting
content:
JavaScript: 7. var and Hoisting

Variables declared with var are function-scoped and hoisted to the top of their scope, initialized as undefined. This causes unpredictable behavior, which is why modern JS strictly uses let and const.

Example:
<code class=
>undefined

topic: 8. Block Scoping and the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
content:
JavaScript: 8. Block Scoping & TDZ

let and const are block-scoped (confined to {}). Accessing them before their declaration line throws a ReferenceError due to the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).

Example:
<code class=
>active

Example:

JavaScript: 10. Primitive Data Types

JavaScript has 7 primitive types: String, Number, BigInt, Boolean, Undefined, Null, and Symbol. Primitives are immutable and passed by value, meaning changes to one variable don't affect copied variables.

Template literals (using backticks) allow multi-line strings and string interpolation via ${}. Tagged templates allow you to parse template literals with a custom function for advanced formatting or escaping.

The Math object provides static properties and methods for mathematical constants and functions. Combined with Number methods like Number.isFinite(), it handles complex numeric operations safely.

In boolean contexts (like if statements), JS coerces values to Booleans. The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n,

Example:

undefined means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value. null is an intentional assignment representing the absence of any object value. Use null to explicitly wipe a reference.

object

Symbol is a primitive type representing a completely unique identifier. Symbols are heavily used as hidden or non-colliding object keys, ensuring properties don't clash during iteration or inheritance.

JavaScript: 18. The typeof operator

typeof returns a string indicating the type of the unevaluated operand. It has a notorious historical bug where typeof null === 'object'. Arrays also return 'object'; use Array.isArray() instead.

Example:

To explicitly convert data types, use the global constructors String(), Number(), and Boolean(). This is safer and more readable than relying on operators for coercion.

content:
JavaScript: 20. Implicit Type Coercion

JS automatically coerces types when applying operators to mismatched types. The + operator favors Strings (concatenation), while -, , and / favor Numbers (math calculations).

Example:
<code class=

JavaScript: 21. Arithmetic Operators & Modulo

Standard operators handle math operations, while the modulo operator % returns the remainder of division. Modulo is crucial for determining even/odd numbers or cyclical operations (like wrapping an array index).

Example:
<code class=

>1
true

JavaScript: 22. Unary Operators

Unary operators work on a single operand. ++ and -- increment/decrement values (pre- or post-evaluation). The unary + is a fast, idiomatic way to implicitly cast a string to a number.

Example:
<code class=

>let count = 5;
console.log(count++); // Post-increment: logs 5, then becomes 6
console.log(++count); // Pre-increment: becomes 7, logs 7
console.log(+'100' + 5); // Unary plus converts to Number

Output:
<code class=

JavaScript: 23. Logical Operators

Logical operators evaluate boolean conditions. The NOT operator ! inverses truthiness. Using double NOT !! is a common shorthand to explicitly cast any value to a strict boolean primitive.

Example:
<code class=

>console.log(!true);
console.log(!!

); // Cast truthy string to boolean true
console.log(!!0); // Cast falsy zero to boolean false

>false
true
false

JavaScript: 24. Short-circuit Evaluation

&& and || short-circuit. || returns the first truthy value it encounters, making it useful for default fallbacks. && returns the first falsy value, often used for conditional execution.

Example:
<code class=
>This executes because isValid is true

JavaScript: 25. Nullish Coalescing (??)

The ?? operator returns the right-hand operand ONLY if the left-hand is null or undefined. Unlike ||, it safely allows falsy values like 0 or

to be treated as valid inputs.

Example:
<code class=

>const count = 0;
console.log(count || 10); // 10 (incorrectly overrides 0)

topic: 26. Optional Chaining (?.) for safe object access
content:
JavaScript: 26. Optional Chaining (?.)

Optional chaining ?. allows you to read nested object properties without manually validating each reference in the chain. If a reference is nullish, the expression short-circuits to undefined instead of throwing an error.

Example:
<code class=

JavaScript: 27. Bitwise Operators

Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) treat operands as 32-bit integers. They operate on binary representations directly, which is extremely fast for permissions matrices, flags, or graphics programming.

Example:
<code class=

>const READ = 1;  // 0001
const WRITE = 2; // 0010
let permissions = READ | WRITE; // 0011 (3)
console.log((permissions & WRITE) === WRITE); // Check if has WRITE

<code class=

JavaScript: 28. if/else and block scope

Control flow relies heavily on if/else statements. Variables declared with let or const inside an if block are entirely isolated to that block, preventing state leakage to the outer scope.

Example:
<code class=

>active
idle

topic: 29. The Ternary Operator and ternary chains
content:
JavaScript: 29. The Ternary Operator

The ternary operator condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse is a one-line shorthand for if/else. Ternary chains can replace complex switch blocks, though excessive chaining harms readability.

JavaScript: 30. The switch Statement

switch evaluates an expression and matches strict equality (===) to case clauses. If a break is omitted, execution

to the next case, which can be useful for grouping identical logic.

try wraps code that might throw an exception. catch intercepts the error to prevent the app from crashing. finally always executes, making it perfect for cleanup tasks (like closing loaders).

Use the throw keyword combined with the native Error constructor (or subclasses like TypeError) to halt execution and pass structured stack trace information to a parent catch block.

JavaScript: 33. The Date Object

The Date object represents a single moment in time (milliseconds since the UNIX epoch). Modifying dates natively can be tricky, so extracting discrete components (like getFullYear) is the standard approach.

Arrays are list-like objects. The literal syntax [] is preferred over the Array() constructor, as new Array(3) confusingly creates an empty array with length 3 instead of an array containing the number 3.

JavaScript: 39. splice, reverse, sort

topic: 48. Object Creation and property access (dot vs bracket)
content:
JavaScript: 48. Object Creation & Access

Objects are key-value dictionaries. Dot notation is standard, but bracket notation obj['key'] is required when the key name is stored in a variable or contains spaces.

Example:
<code class=

>Dan
true

JavaScript: 49. Iterating Object Properties

Since objects aren't natively iterable via loops, we use Object.keys() to get an array of keys, Object.values() for values, and Object.entries() for key-value pairs (tuples).

Example:
<code class=

>make: Ford
year: 2020

JavaScript: 50. Object Property Descriptors

Every object property has underlying attributes configuring its behavior. Object.defineProperty() lets you define if a property can be modified (writable), looped over (enumerable), or deleted (configurable).

Example:
<code class=

JavaScript: 51. freeze() vs seal()

Object.freeze() makes an object entirely immutable (no adding, removing, or changing properties). Object.seal() prevents adding or removing properties, but allows modifying existing ones.

Example:
<code class=
>{ theme: 'light' }

JavaScript: 52. Shallow vs Deep Cloning

Using the spread operator { ...obj } creates a shallow copy, meaning nested objects share memory references. To deep clone an object safely, modern JS provides the native structuredClone() function.

Example:
<code class=

JavaScript: 53. Array Destructuring

Array destructuring lets you neatly unpack values from arrays into distinct variables based on index position. It's also a brilliantly concise trick for swapping two variables without a temporary third variable.

Example:
<code class=

JavaScript: 54. Object Destructuring

Object destructuring maps properties into variables by key name rather than order. You can alias the extracted variable names and assign fallback default values if the property is undefined.

topic: 55. The Spread Operator (...) for arrays and objects

JavaScript: 55. The Spread Operator (...)

JavaScript: 56. The Rest Parameter

While structurally identical to the spread operator, the rest parameter (...args) works in reverse: it aggregates leftover arguments passed to a function into a true Array, replacing the legacy arguments object.

content:
JavaScript: 57. The Map object

Unlike standard objects which only allow Strings or Symbols as keys, a Map is a collection that allows keys of ANY type (including objects or functions). Maps also maintain insertion order perfectly.

Example:

topic: 58. The Set object: Enforcing unique values
content:
JavaScript: 58. The Set object

A Set is a collection of entirely unique values. Adding a duplicate item is simply ignored. It's the fastest, most idiomatic way to deduplicate an array by converting it to a Set and back.

Example:

topic: 59. WeakMap and WeakSet: Garbage collection benefits
content:
JavaScript: 59. WeakMap & WeakSet

WeakMap and WeakSet exclusively accept objects as keys/values and hold

references to them. If no other references to the object exist, the memory is garbage-collected automatically, preventing memory leaks.

Example:

topic: 60. ArrayBuffer and raw binary data allocation
content:
JavaScript: 60. ArrayBuffer

An ArrayBuffer represents a generic, fixed-length raw binary data buffer. You cannot manipulate it directly; you must create a TypedArray or a DataView to read and write its memory chunks.

Example:
<code class=
>Buffer byteLength: 4

JavaScript: 61. TypedArrays

TypedArrays provide a view over an ArrayBuffer, locking elements to a specific numeric type (like 8-bit integers or 32-bit floats). They operate with C-like performance, crucial for WebGL and Audio processing.

<code class=

JavaScript: 62. DataView

Unlike TypedArrays which enforce a single data type, a DataView provides a low-level interface for reading and writing multiple different numeric types within the same ArrayBuffer at specific byte offsets.

topic: 63. Blob objects: Representing raw file data
content:
JavaScript: 63. Blob objects

A Blob (Binary Large Object) represents immutable, raw file-like data. They are commonly used to construct downloadable files on the client-side or wrap image data for uploading to an API.

Example:
<code class=
>14 'text/html'

topic: 64. The File object and FileReader API
content:
JavaScript: 64. File and FileReader

The File object inherits from Blob, adding metadata like a filename. The FileReader API asynchronously reads the contents of File/Blob objects, translating them to base64 strings or ArrayBuffers.

Example:
<code class=
>text

JavaScript: 65. Declarations vs Expressions

Function Declarations are fully hoisted, allowing invocation before they appear in code. Function Expressions (assigning a function to a variable) are NOT hoisted, adhering to linear execution logic.

Example:
<code class=
>A

content:
JavaScript: 66. Arrow Functions

Arrow functions () => {} provide concise syntax. If the body is a single expression without braces, the result is implicitly returned. They lack their own this binding, inheriting it lexically.

An IIFE is a function that runs the moment it is defined. Historically used to create private variable scopes before modules and let existed, they are now mainly used for executing top-level async code.

JavaScript: 68. Arguments vs Rest

The legacy arguments object is an array-like object available inside non-arrow functions containing all passed parameters. Modern ES6 prefers the Rest parameter (...args) because it returns a true array with array methods.

ES6 allows default parameter values in function signatures. The default value is applied ONLY if the caller passes exactly undefined (passing null or 0 overrides the default).

content:
JavaScript: 70. The Call Stack

The Call Stack is a LIFO (Last In, First Out) data structure the JS engine uses to track function execution. When a function finishes, it is popped off the stack. Excessive recursion causes a Stack Overflow.

<code class=
>AB

content:
JavaScript: 71. The Execution Context

Every time a function runs, an Execution Context is created, consisting of a Variable Environment (its local variables) and a reference to its outer lexical environment. This context is what powers scoping rules.

JavaScript: 72. Lexical Scoping

Lexical Scoping means inner functions have access to variables defined in their outer scope based on exactly where the function was structurally written in the source code, not where it is called from.

Example:

A Closure occurs when a function

the variables in its lexical scope even after the outer function has returned. The inner function maintains a persistent link to that environment's memory.

content:
JavaScript: 74. Closures for Data Privacy

Before ES6 classes introduced private fields, closures were the standard way to achieve encapsulation. Variables scoped inside the outer function act as entirely private variables, manipulated only by the returned methods.

100

Memoization is an optimization technique using closures to cache expensive function results. By storing previous inputs and outputs in a hidden closure object, repeated calls return the cached data instantly.

content:
JavaScript: 76. Closure Memory Leaks

Because closures retain outer references indefinitely, attaching a closure to a long-lived object (like the DOM window) can prevent garbage collection of large datasets. Fix this by nullifying heavy variables when done.

Example:
<code class=
>Memory freed (No visible output)

A Pure Function always yields the exact same output for the same input and causes zero

(it doesn't modify external state, network, or DOM). This makes them incredibly predictable and testable.

Example:
<code class=

A Higher-Order Function (HOF) is any function that takes another function as an argument (like map or filter) OR returns a function. They allow abstracting behaviors rather than just values.

JavaScript: 79. Currying

Currying is transforming a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument. It leverages closures to create specialized utility functions on the fly.

topic: 80. The this keyword: Default and implicit binding
content:
JavaScript: 80. The this keyword

In JS, this resolves dynamically based on HOW a function is called, not where it is written. In implicit binding, this points to the object to the left of the dot calling the method.

Example:
<code class=

You can override the default this context explicitly using call() or apply(). call takes arguments sequentially, while apply expects an array of arguments.

Example:

Unlike call or apply which execute the function immediately, bind() returns a NEW function permanently bound to the specified this context, protecting it from being overridden later.

Arrow functions do NOT have their own this binding. Instead, they lexically inherit this from their parent scope. This makes them perfect for callbacks inside class methods, but terrible for defining object methods.

JavaScript objects inherit properties through a Prototype Chain. If a property isn't found on the object itself, JS traverses up to the object's hidden proto link until it hits null.

Standard imports execute synchronously on load. Dynamic imports import() return a Promise and load modules asynchronously during runtime. This is the cornerstone of lazy-loading and code splitting in frameworks like React.

topic: 102. The Event Loop and single-threaded execution
content:
JavaScript: 102. The Event Loop

JS is purely single-threaded. The Event Loop monitors the Call Stack and the Task Queues. If the Call Stack is empty, it pushes the next pending asynchronous callback onto the stack, allowing non-blocking I/O.

Example:
<code class=

>1. Start
2. End
3. Timeout

JavaScript: 103. Microtasks vs Macrotasks

Promises run in the Microtask queue, which has absolute priority over the Macrotask queue (setTimeout, DOM events). After a synchronous execution completes, the Event Loop empties ALL Microtasks before handling a single Macrotask.

Example:
<code class=

>Sync
Microtask (Promise)
Macrotask (Timeout)

JavaScript: 104. Callbacks

A callback is a function passed as an argument, executed later. Heavy nesting leads to

More critically, passing a callback hands control of your program to a third-party function (Inversion of Control).

topic: 105. Promises: Pending, Fulfilled, and Rejected states
content:
JavaScript: 105. Promises states

A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion of an async operation. It exists in one of three mutually exclusive states: Pending, Fulfilled (success), or Rejected (error). Once settled, state cannot change.

Example:
<code class=
>Promise { 'Success' }

JavaScript: 106. Constructing Promises

You wrap legacy callback APIs in Promises by invoking the new Promise(executor) constructor. The executor receives resolve and reject arguments to signal when the underlying asynchronous task concludes.

Example:
<code class=
>Timer done

JavaScript: 107. Promise Chaining

Every .then() returns a completely new Promise, allowing for clean, linear chaining. A single .catch() at the end of the chain securely intercepts any rejection that occurred anywhere upstream.

Example:
<code class=

>Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(val => val * 2)
  .then(val => { throw new Error('Failed at ' + val); })
  .catch(err => console.log(err.message));

Output:
<code class=
>Failed at 4

JavaScript: 108. The .finally() method

The .finally() block executes after a Promise settles, regardless of whether it was Fulfilled or Rejected. It is the gold standard for global cleanup operations, like hiding a UI loading spinner.

Example:
<code class=

>Network Error
Loading state: false

JavaScript: 109. Promise.all()

Promise.all() receives an array of Promises and executes them concurrently. It resolves with an array of all results. However, it fails fast: if a single Promise rejects, the entire operation instantly rejects.

Example:
<code class=

JavaScript: 110. race() vs any()

Promise.race() resolves or rejects as soon as the FIRST promise in the array settles. Promise.any() ignores rejections and returns the first successfully Fulfilled promise (useful for pinging multiple redundant servers).

Example:
<code class=
>Fast

JavaScript: 111. Promise.allSettled()

Unlike Promise.all() which short-circuits on a single error, Promise.allSettled() waits for ALL promises to complete, returning an array of objects detailing the status (fulfilled/rejected) and value/reason for each.

Example:
<code class=
>[ 'fulfilled', 'rejected' ]

JavaScript: 112. Async/Await

The await keyword can only be used inside an async function. It syntactically halts the execution of that specific function until the awaited Promise settles, allowing asynchronous code to read like synchronous code.

Example:
<code class=
>Mock Data

topic: 113. Handling errors in Async/Await with try/catch
content:
JavaScript: 113. Errors in Async/Await

Because await unwraps a Promise directly, Promise rejections are thrown as actual exceptions. Wrapping await calls in traditional try/catch blocks is the standard methodology for handling these errors gracefully.

Example:
<code class=
>Caught: 404 Not Found

topic: 114. Sequential vs Parallel execution in Async/Await
content:
JavaScript: 114. Sequential vs Parallel

Awaiting promises back-to-back causes a sequential waterfall (slow). To execute tasks in parallel while using async/await, initiate all promises first, then wrap them in await Promise.all().

>A B

An iterator is an object with a next() method returning { value, done }. This protocol powers all for...of loops and spread syntax. You can consume values manually by invoking next() until done is true.

Declared with function*, generators can pause their own execution via yield and resume later. They automatically act as custom Iterators and are exceptional at managing infinite sequences or custom state machines.

JavaScript: 117. Async Generators

Async generators combine async and function* to yield Promises. The ES2018 for await...of loop smoothly iterates over these streams of asynchronous data, automatically resolving each chunk as it arrives.

JavaScript: 118. Timers

setTimeout executes a callback once after a delay, while setInterval loops endlessly. Both push tasks to the Macrotask queue. The specified time is a MINIMUM delay, not a guarantee, depending on main thread blockage.

Example:
<code class=
>Timer cleared

JavaScript: 119. requestAnimationFrame

Instead of jittery setInterval animations, requestAnimationFrame (rAF) aligns callback execution strictly with the browser's display refresh rate (usually 60fps), drastically improving performance and battery life.

Example:

>Animation frame requested

JavaScript: 120. Debouncing

Debouncing forces a function to wait a certain amount of time before running. If the event fires again before the timer ends, the timer resets. It's critical for search bars and window resizing to prevent API spam.

Example:
<code class=
>Searching API...

JavaScript: 121. Throttling

While debouncing waits for a pause in events, Throttling guarantees execution at a steady, predefined rate (e.g., exactly once every 100ms). It's the standard optimization for scroll and mousemove listeners.

topic: 122. The DOM Tree: Nodes vs Elements
content:
JavaScript: 122. Nodes vs Elements

The DOM (Document Object Model) maps HTML tags to JS objects. While all HTML tags are Elements, the DOM tree also includes Text Nodes (whitespace/text) and Comment Nodes. Methods like children return only Elements, ignoring raw text nodes.

Example:
<code class=
>DOM conceptually mapped

JavaScript: 123. Selecting Elements

getElementById is highly optimized and fast. However, querySelector (and querySelectorAll) is the modern standard, allowing you to fetch DOM elements using complex, standard CSS selector strings.

Example:
<code class=
>// const btn = document.querySelector('.btn-primary[data-active=
>Selected element matching CSS rules

JavaScript: 124. Creating & Appending DOM

Use document.createElement() to build detached nodes in memory. Modifying them offline is fast. You then inject them into the live DOM tree using modern methods like append() or prepend().

Example:
<code class=
>Appended div to DOM

JavaScript: 125. Removing Elements

Historically, removing an element required referencing its parent (parent.removeChild(child)). Modern browsers support the child.remove() method directly, simplifying element destruction.

Example:
<code class=
>Modal element completely removed from DOM tree

JavaScript: 126. DocumentFragment

Injecting thousands of elements directly into the live DOM causes severe layout thrashing (reflows). A DocumentFragment is a lightweight, invisible DOM node. You append children to it in memory, then append the fragment once to the live DOM.

Example:
<code class=
>Batched DOM update complete

JavaScript: 127. Bubbling and Capturing

Events flow in two phases. In Capturing, the event travels DOWN from the Window to the target. In Bubbling (default behavior), it travels UP from the target back to the Window, triggering listeners on ancestors along the way.

Example:
<code class=

>Child Click
Parent Bubble

JavaScript: 128. stopPropagation vs preventDefault

preventDefault() stops the browser's native action (like following a link or submitting a form). stopPropagation() stops the event from bubbling up the DOM tree to parent listeners, effectively isolating the click.

Example:

JavaScript: 129. Event Delegation

Instead of attaching listeners to 1,000 dynamic list items, attach ONE listener to the parent ul. Use the bubbling e.target to detect which specific child was clicked. It saves massive amounts of memory.

Example:
<code class=
>Delegated event processed successfully

JavaScript: 130. CustomEvent objects

You can trigger synthetic, programmatic events in the browser using the CustomEvent constructor. By passing a detail object, you can broadcast structured payload data seamlessly across disjointed UI components.

Example:
<code class=
>Custom event authSuccess dispatched

The Shadow DOM attaches a hidden, heavily encapsulated DOM tree to a custom element. Styles defined inside the shadow root CANNOT leak out, and global CSS CANNOT leak in, ensuring pristine visual isolation.

JavaScript: 138. Templates & Slots

The <template> tag holds inert HTML that the browser parses but doesn't render. When combined with Shadow DOM, <slot> tags act as placeholders allowing developers to dynamically inject custom user content into predefined layouts.

JavaScript: 139. The Fetch API

fetch() is the modern, Promise-based native standard for network requests, heavily replacing XMLHttpRequest. By default, it issues GET requests. Passing an options object configures it for POSTs and body payloads.

JavaScript: 141. Fetch Headers

You configure HTTP headers in Fetch by supplying a headers object. Setting Content-Type: application/json is strictly mandatory when sending JSON payloads, and Authorization headers securely pass Bearer tokens to APIs.
